summary:
Allwork.Space reports on an August 27 memorandum from the U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM) encouraging federal agencies to use AI across the hiring lifecycle, from drafting job announcements to screening applications and evaluating candidates. OPM frames adoption as an efficiency measure tied to the federal goal of cutting average time to hire to 80 days, and it clarifies when AI-assisted hiring counts as "high-impact" under existing federal AI policy.

The central distinction is between AI supporting a decision and AI output becoming the basis for it. OPM says AI-assisted hiring generally is not high-impact where an authorized official independently reviews the underlying evidence, evaluates the reasoning, and makes the final determination on that record. A formal human sign-off alone is insufficient: if officials merely ratify an AI recommendation without examining underlying information, the AI output can still be treated as the principal basis for the decision, making the use high-impact.

Permitted lower-scrutiny uses include drafting position descriptions, job announcements and interview questions, plus resume screening, qualification reviews and candidate summaries, provided officials review the underlying application materials and reach their own determinations. Higher scrutiny applies to AI recommendations that an applicant fails minimum qualifications, candidate matching, and scoring or ranking systems, because these directly affect access to federal employment. These are presumed high-impact, though agencies may document a basis for concluding otherwise.

Even for non-high-impact uses, agencies must correctly apply veterans' preference, meet accessibility and reasonable-accommodation requirements, use authorized systems with appropriate privacy protections, and keep auditable records. Applicants retain existing avenues to challenge adverse eligibility decisions.

OPM said it will keep adding AI capabilities to federal hiring tools including USA Staffing, USAJOBS, USA Hire, USA Class and USA Performance. Responsibility for hiring decisions remains with agency officials, who must be able to explain and support their determinations.
